rejected.title: Using economic terms in explanations
card: An economic explanation says what happened and why. It uses the correct economic terms, not everyday words that are vague.
Economic terms
Words such as demand (how much buyers want a good at different prices) and opportunity cost (the next best option given up) have exact meanings. Using them correctly makes a claim clear.
Evidence
Each claim should be backed by data from a named source, such as a figure from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS). Naming the source lets a reader check it.
A strong explanation joins the two: it makes a claim with the right term, then gives the data and its source. A claim with no data, or data with no source, is weaker.
rejected.remember: Use the right term for each idea, and back each claim with data from a named source.

a.q: Which sentence is the clearest economic explanation?
opts: Demand for electric bikes rose 15% in 2023, says the ABS
Lots of people suddenly seemed to want electric bikes
Electric bikes are a really popular thing these days
Everyone I know has bought an electric bike lately
a.why: It uses the term demand and backs the claim with a figure from a named source, the ABS. The others use vague words and give no data or source, so a reader cannot check them.
a.clue: Look for a correct term plus data from a named source.

b.q: Priya says: "Skipping the school fair to work cost me the fair, which was my opportunity cost." She then adds that her shift paid $96, according to her payslip. Which change would best improve her explanation?
opts: Name the source of the claim about the fair's popularity
Replace opportunity cost with a more everyday phrase
Remove the payslip figure so the claim is shorter
Use demand instead of opportunity cost for the fair
b.why: Her use of opportunity cost is correct, since the fair is the next best option she gave up, and her pay figure has a named source. Any new claim, such as how popular the fair was, would need a named source too. Dropping the term or the data would make the explanation weaker.
b.clue: Priya already uses the term correctly. What would any new claim need?

proposal.title: Using economic terms in explanations
card: An economic explanation says what happened and why. It uses the correct economic terms, not everyday words that are vague.
Economic terms

Words such as demand (the amount of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices) and opportunity cost (the next best option given up) have exact meanings. Using them correctly makes a claim clear.
Evidence

Each claim should be backed by data from a named source, such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) or a local council. Naming the source lets a reader check it. "A post I saw online" does not name a source.
A strong explanation joins the two: it makes a claim with the right term, then gives the data and its source. A claim with no data, or data with no source, is weaker.
proposal.remember: Use the right term for each idea, and back each claim with data from a named source.

a.q: An Ashvale Council survey found that buyers in Ashvale bought 15% more bikes in 2023. Which sentence is the clearest economic explanation?
opts: Bike demand rose 15% in 2023, says Ashvale Council
Bikes got 15% more popular in 2023, says Ashvale Council
Bike demand rose 15% in 2023, says a post I saw online
Bike opportunity cost rose 15% in 2023, says Ashvale Council
a.why: It uses the correct term, demand, for what buyers bought, and it names the council as its source. The popular option uses a vague everyday word, and the online post is not a named source. Opportunity cost is the wrong term, because it means the next best option given up.
a.clue: Check both the term and the source in each sentence.

b.q: Priya says: "Skipping the school fair to work cost me the fair, which was my opportunity cost." She then adds that her shift paid $96, according to her payslip. Which change would best improve her explanation?
opts: If she adds a claim about the fair, name its source
Replace opportunity cost with a more everyday phrase
Remove the payslip figure so the claim is shorter
Use demand instead of opportunity cost for the fair
b.why: Her use of opportunity cost is correct, since the fair is the next best option she gave up, and her pay figure has a named source. Any new claim she adds about the fair would need a named source too. Swapping the term for an everyday phrase or the wrong term, or dropping the data, would make the explanation weaker.

version.title: Using economic terms in explanations
card: An economic explanation says what happened and why. It makes a claim, gives a reason, and backs it up.
Demand
how much buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices. It is not the same as the number sold.
Opportunity cost
the next best option given up when you make a choice. It is what you give up, not what you gain.
Evidence
data that backs a claim, with its source named, such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics. A reader can then check it, so data with no source is weaker.
version.remember: Use each term for its exact meaning, and back each claim with data from a named source.

a.q: Students explain why more people in their town bought bikes this year. Which explanation is clearest?
opts: Fuel cost 20% more (council data), so demand for bikes rose
Bike sales rose 20% (council data), so bike demand rose 20%
Fuel cost about 20% more, so the demand for bikes rose a lot
Fuel got much dearer, so heaps more people wanted bikes
a.why: It uses demand correctly, since dearer fuel makes people willing to buy more bikes at each price, and it gives a figure with a named source. The sales option has data and a source too, but it treats demand as the number sold.
a.clue: Check how each option uses the word demand, then look for data and a source.

b.q: Priya writes: "I skipped the school fair to work a shift. My payslip shows it paid $96, so $96 was my opportunity cost." Which change would best improve her explanation?
opts: Name the fair as her opportunity cost
Drop the payslip, since sources are not needed
Call the $96 her demand for work instead
Swap opportunity cost for an everyday word
b.why: Opportunity cost is the next best option given up, and Priya gave up the fair. The $96 is what she gained by working, so calling it her opportunity cost misuses the term. Her payslip is a named source, so it should stay.
b.clue: What did Priya give up when she chose to work?

a.best: Fuel cost 20% more (council data), so demand for bikes rose

b.best: Name the fair as her opportunity cost
